nameStory: The Baltimore checkerspot got its distinctive name from the first Lord Baltimore, George Calvert, who founded the Maryland colony in the 1600s. The butterfly's bold pattern of black, orange, and white perfectly matched the colors on the Baltimore family coat of arms. This royal connection made it a natural choice when Maryland selected it as their official state insect in 1973.
description: The Baltimore checkerspot is a medium-sized butterfly with a wingspan of about 2-2.5 inches that displays a striking checkerboard pattern. Its wings feature bold blocks of black, bright orange-red, and creamy white arranged in a geometric design that looks almost like a stained glass window. The upper wings are primarily black with orange patches near the body and white spots along the outer edges, while the underwings show more intricate patterns of orange, white, and black checks. This eye-catching butterfly belongs to the brush-footed butterfly family, meaning its front legs are reduced and brush-like rather than used for walking.

idTips.label: Checkerboard wing pattern
idTips.description: Look for the unmistakable pattern of black, orange, and white squares arranged like a checkerboard across the wings, with the colors forming distinct blocks rather than gradual transitions

idTips.label: Orange body markings
idTips.description: The body appears fuzzy to the touch and shows bright orange-red patches near where the wings attach, contrasting sharply with the black base color

idTips.label: White wing borders
idTips.description: The outer edges of both upper and lower wings feature neat rows of white spots that feel slightly raised when touched, creating a distinct border pattern

idTips.label: Medium butterfly size
idTips.description: About the size of your palm when wings are spread, noticeably larger than a quarter but smaller than most swallowtail butterflies

idTips.label: Brush-footed legs
idTips.description: When landed, appears to stand on only four legs since the front pair are tiny and brush-like, held close to the body and used for tasting rather than walking

habitat: Baltimore checkerspots prefer wet meadows, marshes, and boggy areas where their caterpillars' favorite food plants grow. Look for them in areas with turtlehead, plantain, and white ash near streams, pond edges, and seasonally flooded meadows. They're most commonly found in areas that stay moist through the growing season, from sea level up to moderate elevations throughout New England.

seasonality.spring: Adults are not yet active, but overwintering caterpillars begin feeding again on warm days in late spring after spending winter in silk shelters.
seasonality.summer: Peak flight time occurs from late May through July when adults are most active, mating, and laying eggs on host plants in wet meadows.
seasonality.fall: Young caterpillars feed actively before creating communal silk webs where they'll spend the winter months in a semi-dormant state.
seasonality.winter: Caterpillars overwinter in silk shelters, remaining inactive until temperatures warm in spring.

funFact: Despite being Maryland's official state insect since 1973, the Baltimore checkerspot has become so rare in Maryland that it's now listed as threatened and endangered there, making it one of the few state symbols that's actually disappearing from the state it represents!
confusionNotes: Baltimore checkerspots are most likely confused with other checkerspot butterflies, but their specific combination of orange, black, and white in distinct blocks (rather than spots or crescents) sets them apart. Remember: Baltimore checkerspots have BLOCKS of color like the Baltimore family crest, while other checkerspots have more scattered spotting patterns.
contextualKnowledge: The butterfly's royal naming connection reflects early American colonial history, when the Calvert family's heraldic colors of black, orange, and white represented their authority in the New World. Ironically, this butterfly named for Maryland's founder is now thriving better in New England than in Maryland itself due to habitat loss in its namesake state.
compareHints: The Baltimore checkerspot is the only member of its genus found in New England, making it unique among our regional checkerspots. Compared to other brush-footed butterflies in the area, it's distinguished by its geometric block pattern rather than the flowing bands of monarchs or the eyespots of wood nymphs. Its checkerboard design is more rigid and angular than the softer patterns found on crescents, tortoiseshells, or fritillaries.
